bibliography.abstract: Non-exhaust emissions from brake and tyre wear are now the dominant source of traffic-related particulate matter, complicated by heavier electric vehicles. Such particulate also includes road-surface wear and resuspended dust, but Dublin’s frequent rain suppresses them, so we calibrate the two dominant channels: brake wear (ultrafine particles, UFP) and tyre wear (PM 2.5 ). We build a high-resolution, moving-observer agent-based model of the Phibsborough junction, Dublin, calibrated against street-level Google Air View data, to evaluate passenger-preserving policy scenarios. Global sensitivity analysis reveals an interaction-dominated system where traffic dynamics rival fleet composition. Electrification benefits depend entirely on regenerative braking: UFP at 50% spans −19% (with regen) to + 13% (without), while PM 2.5 rises 1 to 5% from added mass. Bus modal shift gives the largest dual-pollutant gains (−30% UFP, −34% PM 2.5 at 50%). A 30 km/h limit cuts UFP 16.5% independently of fleet; a combined policy delivers −27% UFP and −12% PM 2.5 .

en.caveats: The model is calibrated for a single, highly specific urban junction in Dublin and assumes frequent rain suppresses road-surface wear and resuspended dust, which may limit generalizability to drier climates.
en.what: An agent-based model of the Phibsborough junction in Dublin, calibrated against street-level Google Air View data, simulates traffic-related ultrafine particles (UFP) from brake wear and PM2.5 from tyre wear. The model evaluates passenger-preserving policy scenarios, showing that a 50% electrification rate only reduces UFP by 19% if regenerative braking is used, while increasing PM2.5 by 1% to 5% due to heavier vehicle mass. In contrast, a 50% bus modal shift reduces UFP by 30% and PM2.5 by 34%, while a 30 km/h speed limit cuts UFP by 16.5% regardless of fleet composition.
en.why: It demonstrates that fleet electrification alone cannot solve traffic-related particulate pollution due to the offsetting effects of vehicle mass on tyre wear, establishing that modal shifts and speed limits are necessary to achieve substantial dual-pollutant reductions.
